apmo-1995-01.title: Add all the inequalities
apmo-1995-01.body:
For the square roots to be defined we need $a_n\ge n-1$ for every $n$. Put
$$b_n=\sqrt{a_n-(n-1)}\ \ge 0,\qquad\text{so}\qquad a_n=b_n^2+(n-1).$$

**Rewrite the conditions.** For $n=1,\dots,1994$ the right-hand side is $a_{n+1}-(n-1)=b_{n+1}^2+n-(n-1)=b_{n+1}^2+1$, so the conditions read
$$2b_n\ge b_{n+1}^2+1\quad(n=1,\dots,1994),$$
and the last condition is $2b_{1995}\ge a_1+1=b_1^2+1$.

**Add them.** Summing all $1995$ inequalities, every $b_k^2$ appears exactly once on the right:
$$2\sum_{n=1}^{1995} b_n\ \ge\ \sum_{n=1}^{1995} b_n^2+1995,
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sum_{n=1}^{1995}(b_n-1)^2\le 0 .$$
Hence $b_n=1$ for every $n$, that is, $a_n-(n-1)=1$, so $a_n=n$.

**Check.** For $a_n=n$: $2\sqrt{n-(n-1)}=2=(n+1)-(n-1)$ for $n\le1994$, and $2\sqrt{1995-1994}=2=a_1+1$. All conditions hold (with equality).

**Answer:** the only sequence is $a_n=n$ ($n=1,\dots,1995$). ∎

apmo-1995-02.title: Pigeonhole on the prime factors
apmo-1995-02.body:
**$n=13$ is not enough.** The $13$ numbers
$$2\cdot101,\ 3\cdot97,\ 5\cdot89,\ 7\cdot83,\ 11\cdot79,\ 13\cdot73,\ 17\cdot71,\ 19\cdot67,\ 23\cdot61,\ 29\cdot59,\ 31\cdot53,\ 37\cdot47,\ 41\cdot43$$
equal $202, 291, 445, 581, 869, 949, 1207, 1273, 1403, 1711, 1643, 1739, 1763$, all between $2$ and $1995$. They are products of two distinct primes, and the $26$ primes used are all different, so the numbers are pairwise coprime. None of them is prime.

**$n=14$ is enough.** Suppose $a_1,\dots,a_{14}$ satisfy (i), (ii) and none is prime. Then each $a_i$ is a product of at least two distinct primes; choose two of them from each $a_i$. Because the $a_i$ are pairwise coprime, no prime divides two different $a_i$, so these $28$ primes are all distinct.

List the $28$ primes in increasing order. The $14$th prime number is $43$, so the $14$th of our primes is at least $43$, and the $15$ primes in positions $14,15,\dots,28$ are all $\ge 43$. These $15$ primes are spread over only $14$ numbers $a_i$, so by the pigeonhole principle some $a_i$ is divisible by two of them. Two distinct primes $\ge43$ have product at least $43\cdot47=2021>1995$, so $a_i>1995$ — a contradiction.

So the smallest $n$ is $14$.

**Remark.** The reading "distinct primes" matters: if prime powers were allowed, the $14$ squares $2^2,3^2,5^2,\dots,43^2=1849$ would be pairwise coprime and composite, and the answer would be $15$ (the smallest prime factors of $15$ pairwise coprime composites are $15$ distinct primes, one of them $\ge47$, and then that number is $\ge47^2=2209$).

**Answer: 14**

apmo-1995-03.title: Radical axes
apmo-1995-03.body:
Let $\omega$ be the circle $PQRS$ and $T$ the intersection of the lines $PQ$ and $RS$. Since $PQ$ and $RS$ are opposite sides of the convex cyclic quadrilateral, $T$ lies outside $\omega$, with $P,Q$ on the same side of $T$ and $R,S$ on the same side of $T$; by the power of the point $T$,
$$TP\cdot TQ=TR\cdot TS=r^2>0 .$$
Let $\Omega$ be the circle with centre $T$ and radius $r$, and let $\Omega^*$ be $\Omega$ without its (four) points lying on the lines $PQ$ and $RS$. We show that the tangency points are exactly the points of $\Omega^*$.

(The circle $\omega$ itself passes through $P,Q,R,S$, so it belongs to both families; if one regards $\omega$ as "tangent to itself", every point of $\omega$ is added to $A$, as in the official solution. Below we consider two different circles.)

**Every tangency point lies on $\Omega^*$.** Let $\Gamma_1\ni P,Q$ and $\Gamma_2\ni R,S$ be different circles tangent at $V$. A tangency point of a circle through $P,Q$ cannot lie on line $PQ$ other than at $P$ or $Q$, and similarly for $RS$; we check below that $V\ne P,Q,R,S$, so $V\in\Omega$ will give $V\in\Omega^*$.

If $\Gamma_1=\omega$, then $\Gamma_2$ meets $\omega$ in the two points $R,S$, so it cannot be tangent to $\omega$ unless $\Gamma_2=\omega=\Gamma_1$; so $\Gamma_1\ne\omega$ and likewise $\Gamma_2\ne\omega$. The radical axis of $\Gamma_1$ and $\omega$ is the line $PQ$, that of $\Gamma_2$ and $\omega$ is the line $RS$, and that of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ is their common tangent $t$ at $V$. The three radical axes of three circles are concurrent or parallel; $PQ$ and $RS$ meet at $T$, so $T\in t$. The power of $T$ with respect to $\Gamma_1$ is then both $TP\cdot TQ$ and $TV^2$ (as $TV$ is tangent to $\Gamma_1$), so $TV=r$, i.e. $V\in\Omega$. Finally $V\ne P$: otherwise $P\in\Gamma_2$, and $\Gamma_2$ would meet $\omega$ in $P,R,S$, so $\Gamma_2=\omega$. Similarly $V\ne Q,R,S$. Thus $V\in\Omega^*$.

**Every point of $\Omega^*$ is a tangency point.** Let $V\in\Omega^*$. As $V$ is not on line $PQ$, there is a unique circle $\Gamma_1$ through $P,Q,V$; similarly $\Gamma_2$ through $R,S,V$. The line $TV$ meets $\Gamma_1$ at $V$ and at a second point $V'$ (possibly $V'=V$), and by the power of $T$: $TV\cdot TV'=TP\cdot TQ=r^2=TV^2$, with $V,V'$ on the same side of $T$ (the power is positive). Hence $V'=V$ and $TV$ is tangent to $\Gamma_1$ at $V$. In the same way $TV$ is tangent to $\Gamma_2$ at $V$. Two circles tangent to the same line at the same point are tangent to each other there, so $V\in A$. (If $\Gamma_1=\Gamma_2$, this circle contains $P,Q,R,S$, so it is $\omega$; this happens exactly for the two points of $\Omega\cap\omega$, which are then only "degenerate" tangency points.)

**Answer:** with $T=PQ\cap RS$, the tangency points of two different circles are the points of the circle with centre $T$ and radius $\sqrt{TP\cdot TQ}$, except its four points on lines $PQ$, $RS$ and its two points on circle $PQRS$. If, as in the official solution, circle $PQRS$ is counted as tangent to itself, all points of circle $PQRS$ are added to $A$. ∎

apmo-1995-04.title: Vectors from the centre
apmo-1995-04.body:
Use vectors with origin $O$; write $X$ for the position vector of a point $X$, and $s=|S|=OS<R$.

**All four points lie on one circle.** In the rectangle $SAMB$ we have $M=A+B-S$. The chords are perpendicular at $S$, so $(A-S)\cdot(B-S)=0$, i.e.
$$A\cdot B-A\cdot S-B\cdot S=-|S|^2 .$$
Therefore, using $|A|=|B|=R$,
$$|M|^2=|A|^2+|B|^2+|S|^2+2(A\cdot B-A\cdot S-B\cdot S)=2R^2+s^2-2s^2=2R^2-s^2 .$$
Each of $N'=B+A'-S$, $M'=A'+B'-S$, $N=B'+A-S$ is formed in exactly the same way from one endpoint of each chord, and $SA'\perp SB$, $SA'\perp SB'$, $SB'\perp SA$, so the same computation gives $|N'|^2=|M'|^2=|N|^2=2R^2-s^2$. So all these points lie on the circle $\Gamma$ with centre $O$ and radius $\rho=\sqrt{2R^2-s^2}$ (note $\rho>R>s$).

**Every point of $\Gamma$ occurs.** Let $X\in\Gamma$ and let $K$ be the midpoint of $SX$; note $X\ne S$ because $|X|=\rho>s$. We look for a position with $M=X$, i.e. $A+B=S+X=2K$ with $SA\perp SB$, i.e. $A,B$ on $C$ symmetric about $K$ and on the circle $\kappa$ with centre $K$ through $S$ (Thales). Let $d=KS=\frac12|X-S|>0$. By the parallelogram law,
$$OK^2+d^2=\frac{|S+X|^2+|X-S|^2}{4}=\frac{|S|^2+|X|^2}{2}=\frac{s^2+2R^2-s^2}{2}=R^2 .$$
So $OK<R$, and the chord of $C$ through $K$ perpendicular to $OK$ (any chord through $K$ if $K=O$) has half-length $\sqrt{R^2-OK^2}=d$; its endpoints $A,B$ satisfy $KA=KB=d$, i.e. they are the ends of a diameter of $\kappa$. Since $S\in\kappa$ and $S\ne A,B$ ($S$ is inside $C$), Thales gives $\angle ASB=90^\circ$. Taking the chords $AA'$, $BB'$ through $S$, the rectangle $SAMB$ has $M=A+B-S=2K-S=X$. As $A$ runs around the whole circle all such configurations occur, so every point of $\Gamma$ is obtained.

**Answer:** the set is the circle with centre $O$ and radius $\sqrt{2R^2-OS^2}$. ∎

apmo-1995-05.title: Construction and a triangle argument
apmo-1995-05.body:
**$k=4$ works.** Define
$$f(x)=1+(x\bmod 2)+2\left(\left\lfloor \tfrac x4\right\rfloor \bmod 2\right)\in\{1,2,3,4\}.$$
The value of $f$ records the pair $\bigl(x\bmod 2,\ \lfloor x/4\rfloor\bmod 2\bigr)$, so $f(x)=f(y)$ only if both entries agree.
- If $|x-y|\in\{5,7\}$, then $x$ and $y$ have different parity, so $f(x)\ne f(y)$.
- If $y=x+12$, then $\lfloor y/4\rfloor=\lfloor x/4\rfloor+3$, which has the other parity, so $f(x)\ne f(y)$.

**$k=3$ is impossible.** Suppose $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\{1,2,3\}$ works. For any $x$, the numbers $x-5$, $x$, $x+7$ have pairwise differences $5,7,12$, so $f(x-5),f(x),f(x+7)$ are the three different values. The number $x+2$ differs from $x-5$ by $7$ and from $x+7$ by $5$, so $f(x+2)\notin\{f(x-5),f(x+7)\}$, forcing $f(x+2)=f(x)$. This holds for every $x$, so
$$f(x)=f(x+2)=f(x+4)=\dots=f(x+12),$$
contradicting $f(x)\ne f(x+12)$. Smaller $k$ are impossible a fortiori.

**Answer: 4**
